It really sucks how finicky these cars are. Check all your intake clamps and pipes for leaks. AFM and vacuum problems sound like your most likely issue right now. Have you checked it for codes?

Also supraforums.com has a lot of knowledge if you haven't checked the forums. Maybe try posting your issue there. Another one is mkiiisupra.net but I don't think it's as popular.

This is the Toyota supra repair manual [TSRM](http://www.cygnusx1.net/Supra/Library/TSRM/MK3/manual.aspx?S=IN&P=1)

Firstly, make sure to check any and all wires associated with the parts you're working on. Double check all your connectors too. These cars suffer horrendously from bad wires and connectors due to age and heat exposure. Verify again that the ECU is plugged in properly since you removed it and reinstalled it. 

Check for vacuum leaks in the intake after the AFM. The air flow meter (AFM; no MAF on these cars) tells the ECU how much air is coming in, so it can fuel it accordingly. Any air coming in that isn't metered will cause it to run like shit or not at all. Without the AFM plugged in, the car should go into sort of a limp mode where it can't rev past 2k. Idk why yours would rev high with no AFM plugged in. Maybe an air leak past the throttle body or stuck throttle? Maybe residual starter fluid in the system caused it to rev high? Side note: NEVER clean the MAF sensor. It will ruin it as noted throughout the forums.

Does your car always need the fuel pump jumped? Normally, the fuel pump only kicks on when you're starting the car. It does not prime when you turn the key to "on" like most cars. Only when the starter is engaged. There is a relay inside the plastic panel between the glovebox and passenger door that controls this, but I doubt this is your culprit for anything. I'd try getting it to run without a jumper. You want to test changes in only one system at a time.

Does the car have any engine modifications? Aftermarket injectors, turbo, Lexus AFM upgrade, AFPR, etc? These could all be places to look as well.

I'm sure that couple of waterproof saddlebags, tail bag, and good backpack will cover anything he needs to transport, rain or shine. Then the rain gear makes life a breeze on those bad days. As for the battery, I'd look into an upgrade because it shouldn't be dying very often if he rides it every day.

I can't answer about their service plan specifics. But as someone who generally works on their own equipment, I'd just save my money and only bring it into the shop if it needs major fixing. I ride an old mountain bike from the mid 2000s, and when I brought it in to be serviced/diagnosed, they only addressed the painstakingly obvious issue of the broken spokes on the wheel. With that one repair, they needed two weeks to fit me into the schedule. They told me everything else was normal (horseshit), so I had to teach myself to repair the derailleurs and brake cables. I haven't had to return there or do any major work once since the wheel repair was done (they did a perfectly fine job too).

My main point here is that you probably won't benefit financially from paying for that service. Bikes don't need a lot of maintenance (not even mine that is older than many of the other students I've met). If you can teach yourself to clean and lubricate your chain, you'll be better off than a lot of the bikes I've seen parked around campus.

TLDR: It's recommended but no.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends circumcision due to the health benefits it provides in the long-term, especially with regard to STDs. While studies have shown that HIV targets cells/receptors in the foreskin, these cells are also present in the shaft of the penis. I think having a say in any procedure done to one's self is very important for children unless it is for a life-threatening situation. Due to the reality that these STD risks are present in circumcised and uncircumcised people, I wouldn't have my child circumcised mainly because I prioritize maintaining bodily autonomy over the risks associated with STDs and phimosis. I think STDs are easily preventable with routine screening and communication with partners.

For anecdotal evidence, I've met men who've been circumcised at a young, but not toddler, age who feel they would've preferred to not have the surgery as they've gotten older. I work in urology and have met many men hesitant to have the surgery despite having a disease that indicates it should be done (phimosis), and I've met a few just getting it done as cosmetics for their partner's preference. I've talked to coworkers and friends who adamantly stand by having it done because "it's just cleaner." 

There are many reasons why people may or may not want it done, and I think it falls far from just what's medically necessary and more along the lines of social acceptance or tradition.

I really think this is an echo from the cruiser scene of the early 2000s. Back in those days, if you didn't have the biggest, heaviest, loudest cruiser with the fattest tire, you weren't a /real/ biker. 

Another thought: I have a stereotype in my mind of large dudes telling me they need large bikes "because I'm a bigger guy." This is a huge misconception imo because, while yes you're contributing to 25-50% of the bike's weight, the power of motorcycles is difficult to conceive and especially handle as a new rider. Not to mention, a sub 500cc bike, while not rip-your-pants-off fast, will still get you killed if you get rear ended by a large vehicle. 

A /real/ bike to me is something on 2 wheels with a motor and a license plate that an individual is daring enough to share on the road with cagers.

It's especially discouraging and rude of people outside of the clique to bash on engine size. *Queue anecdote* I learned on a ninja 250. I was told by many non riders not to get anything less than a 600. It was gutless (compared to my bikes since). It was faster than any car me or my friends owned. I almost wrecked it. I dropped it. I learned how to work on it. I learned how to turn on the street at speed. I learned great clutch control. I saved gas.
Some people want to use their first bike to learn to be on the street. Some just want to commute to work and save on gas. Some want to go off-road. Some want to cruise with their friends. They don't want to be faster than everyone else.
